A.title: Gibraltar Names Stephen Hodgson as Gambling Commissioner
A.excerpt: Gibraltar picks ex-Entain tax chief Stephen Hodgson to succeed Andrew Lyman in 2027. What it means for licensees under the Gambling Act 2025.
body: Gibraltar has confirmed that Stephen Hodgson will become its next Gambling Commissioner and Executive Director of the Gambling Division. The announcement, made by Minister Nigel Feetham on 16 November 2026, follows an independent recruitment process run by the Gibraltar Development Corporation, in which the selection panel recommended Mr Hodgson unanimously. He will succeed Andrew Lyman, who has led the regulator since 2018, when Mr Lyman's tenure ends in early 2027. The appointment remains subject to any necessary regulatory pre-approvals.

The choice is notable for the candidate's background. Mr Hodgson is currently Vice President of Tax at Midnite and spent more than eight years at Entain, including as Deputy Group Tax Director. He chaired the Betting and Gaming Council's Tax Committee from 2017 until February 2026. Gibraltar has therefore selected a commissioner from the industry side, with deep expertise in fiscal policy and international markets, rather than a career regulator. The Minister framed the appointment as one that will help the sector expand its international reach, and Mr Hodgson has spoken of positioning Gibraltar as a tier one gaming centre of excellence.

The handover comes at a pivotal point in the jurisdiction's regulatory cycle. The Gambling Act 2025 came into force on 1 April 2026 and replaced the historic framework with an activity-based licensing model, under which permissions attach to the regulated activities an operator actually carries on rather than to broad licence categories. Some provisions of the Act, notably those concerning regulated individuals, have not yet been commenced. The incoming commissioner will therefore inherit responsibility for completing implementation, including the regime for personal approvals of key individuals, which will shape governance and fitness-and-propriety obligations across the licensed population.

Mr Lyman's tenure also saw Gibraltar introduce, in July 2026, a dedicated authorisation framework for prediction markets, presented as the first of its kind in a European jurisdiction. How that framework is supervised in practice, and whether Gibraltar seeks to grow it as a distinct line of business, will be an early test of the new leadership. Prediction markets sit at the boundary between gambling and financial services, and the regulator's approach to product classification, consumer protection and anti-money laundering controls will be closely watched by applicants and by other European regulators who remain sceptical of the product.

For operators, the commercial context matters as much as the legal one. Gaming accounts for roughly 30 per cent of Gibraltar's GDP and about a third of its tax receipts, and the jurisdiction's licensees are heavily exposed to the British market, where remote gaming duty increases are squeezing margins. A commissioner with a tax specialism may bring sharper insight into how fiscal changes in Great Britain and elsewhere affect group structures, transfer pricing and the location of functions. That expertise could inform how Gibraltar positions itself to retain substance-based operations as groups reassess where they base staff and decision-making.

There is a governance question that licensees and observers will reasonably raise: the movement of a senior industry executive into the regulator's top post. Gibraltar's model has long emphasised close dialogue with a relatively small number of high-quality licensees, and the Gambling Act 2025 retains that approach. Nevertheless, conflict-of-interest management, recusal arrangements for matters touching former employers, and transparency in decision-making will be important for maintaining the confidence of the UK Gambling Commission and other partner regulators that rely on Gibraltar's supervision when its licensees serve their markets.

Practically, we would not expect an immediate shift in supervisory priorities before the handover. However, operators should use the transition period to ensure their licence permissions accurately reflect the activity-based structure of the new Act, that their key-person and governance documentation is ready for the commencement of the regulated individuals provisions, and that any prediction market or novel product plans are discussed early with the Gambling Division. Groups considering restructuring in response to UK tax changes should take advice on how those changes interact with Gibraltar licensing conditions and substance expectations.

The appointment signals that Gibraltar intends to compete actively for international business while completing a significant legislative overhaul. Whether an industry-experienced commissioner strengthens the jurisdiction's commercial appeal without diluting its regulatory credibility will become clearer during 2027. Licensees should engage constructively with the new leadership and monitor commencement orders, guidance and any revised supervisory framework published as the transition proceeds.

A.title: Uganda's 15% Winnings Tax: Casinos Push GGR Alternative
A.excerpt: Uganda's 15% withholding tax on gaming winnings now covers land-based casinos. Operators want the 30% GGR model kept. The compliance issues.
body: Uganda's land-based casino sector has opened a formal challenge to the way the country now taxes gaming winnings. The Uganda Gaming Operators Association, chaired by Robert Kabonero, is asking for land-based casinos to remain under the existing 30 per cent gross gaming revenue framework rather than being required to apply a 15 per cent withholding tax to individual players' winnings. The association has raised the issue with the Private Sector Foundation Uganda, whose policy department will assess it and prepare an advocacy paper for government.

The legal position is clear for now. The Income Tax (Amendment) Act, 2026, Act 21 of 2026, was assented to on 20 August and gazetted on 28 August, with retrospective effect from 1 July 2026. It imposes a 15 per cent withholding tax on gaming and betting winnings, defined as the payout less the amount staked. During the parliamentary process, a proposed exemption for land-based casino winnings was removed on 4 August, with legislators citing tax avoidance and revenue leakage. The only surviving exemption covers winnings paid by a licensed national lottery operator.

The Uganda Revenue Authority has since published a public notice, first issued on 30 October and updated on 2 November 2026, explaining how the tax is to be calculated. For table games, the taxable amount is chips cashed out minus chips purchased during a visit. For slot machines, it is cash-out minus cash-in. For online gaming, the tax applies to net gains at each withdrawal, and for sports betting it must be withheld before winnings are paid or credited. The notice therefore turns a broad statutory principle into product-specific operational rules, each of which carries its own data and reconciliation burden.

The casino operators' objection is fundamentally practical rather than a rejection of taxation. In an online environment, an operator holds a single account history and can calculate stakes and returns precisely. In a physical casino, players buy chips, move between tables and machines, and redeem at the cage, sometimes in multiple transactions across a visit. The association's example is a player who buys UGX 1 million in chips and cashes out UGX 700,000: a net loss on which no tax is due. Establishing that position reliably, for every player and every visit, requires identification, transaction monitoring and reconciliation systems that many venues do not currently operate.

That burden overlaps with anti-money laundering obligations. Accurate visit-level tracking of chip purchases and redemptions is close to the kind of customer and transaction monitoring that financial crime frameworks expect of casinos, and a tax rule that requires it may in practice accelerate improvements in AML controls. The risk, however, is that the cost falls disproportionately on smaller venues. The association says licensed land-based casinos directly employ more than 2,500 people and warns that higher compliance costs could push some players toward illegal gambling, a familiar argument in African markets where unlicensed provision remains significant.

The association's alternative proposals deserve attention from policymakers. It suggests separate licensing for online and land-based casinos, clearer classification of transactions and separate financial records, independent audits and stronger monitoring, and a joint technical working group with government. Several of these would address the revenue leakage concerns that drove Parliament to remove the exemption, while preserving a GGR-based method that is easier to administer and audit at venue level. Whether the Ministry of Finance is open to such a compromise is uncertain, particularly given that the President and Finance Minister had earlier signalled support for revising the tax treatment of casino winnings.

For operators in Uganda, the immediate priority is compliance with the law as it stands. The withholding obligation applies now, with retrospective effect from 1 July, and failure to withhold and remit exposes operators to penalties and interest under Ugandan tax administration rules. Casinos should document their calculation methodology against the URA notice, implement player identification at the point of chip purchase where they have not already, and retain records that allow visit-level reconstruction. Online and sports betting operators should confirm that their withdrawal and settlement flows apply withholding at the correct point.

International groups with African portfolios should also note the wider trend. Winnings taxes collected at source are increasingly common across the continent and are administratively attractive to revenue authorities, but they shift collection risk and systems cost onto operators. Uganda's experience illustrates the importance of engaging during the drafting stage, when product-specific exemptions and methodologies can still be negotiated. Operators should take local tax advice and consider coordinated industry representations if they wish to influence any review.

A.title: Egypt's Digital Safety Law: Criminalising Online Betting
A.excerpt: Egypt will fold its online betting crackdown into a Digital Safety Law due in Parliament by mid-December. Who faces liability, and the risks.
body: Egypt has changed the vehicle for its long-promised crackdown on online betting. Rather than enacting a standalone betting statute or a narrow amendment to its cybercrime legislation, the government now intends to address online gambling through a broader Digital Safety Law. On 1 November 2026, Ahmed Badawi, chair of the House of Representatives' Communications and Information Technology Committee, said the government expects to send the bill to Parliament in about six weeks, which points to mid-December. The draft has not been published, so the precise scope of its betting provisions remains unknown.

The timetable should be treated with caution. In May, Mr Badawi said amendments to the Cybercrime Law would reach Parliament within a month; they did not. In early October, he said his committee would open the new session with the bill and complete its work within a month. Repeated slippage is common where legislation is consolidated into broader packages, and the Digital Safety Law will also include rules on children's social media use and protections for adults against technology risks. Operators and their counsel should plan for the law arriving, but not assume a fixed date.

The legal starting point is already restrictive. Egypt has no licensed online gambling market. Under the Civil Code, gambling contracts are void, and the Penal Code targets gambling premises. The only lawful casino gaming takes place in licensed hotel casinos, which, under the 2022 hotel and tourism legislation, may admit only foreign passport holders. Offshore sites have nevertheless been widely accessed, frequently via VPNs, and authorities have relied on blocking: by May 2026, 70 betting apps had been blocked through the National Telecom Regulatory Authority working with the Supreme Council for Media Regulation.

What is new is the intended shift from blocking to personal criminal liability. Mr Badawi has said the law will go beyond blocking websites and apps, because operators keep relaunching platforms under new domains. The targets he has described include betting brokers and their representatives inside Egypt, anyone who promotes the platforms, and anyone who helps citizens to access them. The planned Cybercrime Law amendments, which will be folded into the new bill, were described in May as carrying up to seven years' imprisonment and fines of EGP 500,000 for creating an app used in cybercrime. Mr Badawi has pointed to the Cybercrime Law's heaviest penalties, which reach life imprisonment, as a model.

That breadth has significant implications for the supply chain. Local agents and cash collectors are the obvious targets, but promotion and facilitation offences could reach affiliates, influencers, payment intermediaries and potentially technology providers whose services are used to reach Egyptian players. International operators that do not market in Egypt but accept Egyptian traffic should not assume that offshore location provides adequate protection, particularly if they rely on local payment agents or marketing partners. Where personal liability attaches to facilitators, those partners will become far more cautious, and the effective availability of offshore products may contract sharply.

Financial crime enforcement is moving in parallel. On 3 November, the Interior Ministry's public funds and organised crime unit took legal action against four suspects over approximately EGP 50 million in alleged laundering from betting and cryptocurrency speculation, and the Public Funds Prosecution subsequently ordered a further arrest and the seizure of defendants' phones. Although the ministry did not specify whether the betting was online, the case shows authorities are prepared to pursue gambling-related proceeds through money laundering charges even before new legislation is in place.

For licensed operators in regulated jurisdictions, the practical response is to review exposure now. Malta, Curaçao and other licensing regimes increasingly expect operators to respect the laws of target markets and to evidence that they are not actively soliciting players where gambling is prohibited. Operators should assess Egyptian traffic and revenue, geolocation and payment controls, affiliate agreements and any local service arrangements. Affiliates and marketing partners should audit campaigns that reach Egyptian audiences, including Arabic-language content distributed through social media.

Egypt's approach reflects a broader pattern in markets that prohibit online gambling: frustration with the limits of domain blocking is leading to laws that target people, money and promotion instead. Once the draft is published, the key issues to analyse will be the definitions of facilitation and promotion, the territorial reach of the offences, and whether intermediaries such as payment providers and platforms face specific duties. Businesses with any Egyptian touchpoint should take local advice as soon as the text becomes available.

A.title: Finland's July 2027 Opening: Is the Regulator Ready?
A.excerpt: A Finnish MP who drove liberalisation warns the new regulator is not yet ready for July 2027. What licence applicants should plan for now.
body: One of the architects of Finland's gambling liberalisation has publicly questioned whether the new regulator will be ready when the market opens. Speaking at SiGMA Rome in early November 2026, Sinuhe Wallinheimo, a National Coalition Party MP and one of the reform's original drivers, said that the authority is still being set up, that the responsible unit is still being formed and hiring, and that the regulator does not yet exist in operational form. His comments, together with an op-ed by Finnish compliance lawyer Antti Koivula arguing that the new regulator may lack capacity, have brought the question of supervisory readiness to the centre of the market entry debate.

The legal timetable is fixed. Finland's online market for casino and betting is due to open to licensed private operators on 1 July 2027, ending Veikkaus's online monopoly while preserving its exclusivity over land-based gaming, scratchcards and the lottery. Responsibility for gambling supervision will move from the National Police Board to a new unit within the Finnish Supervisory Agency on the launch date. The same unit will process licence applications. B2C licensing has already opened, and the B2B supplier licensing window opens on 1 July 2027.

The opening has already slipped once, reportedly because of staffing shortfalls at the supervisory agency, and that history explains why Mr Wallinheimo's comments matter. A regulator that is building its team while simultaneously processing first-wave applications faces an obvious risk of backlogs. For operators, the critical question is whether licences will be granted in time to launch on day one, or whether early entrants will be those that filed first and supplied the most complete applications. Delays at this stage translate directly into lost market share in a market where first-mover positioning matters.

Licensing is moving, nonetheless. SkillOnNet announced in late October that it had secured a Finnish iGaming licence ahead of the 2027 opening, and content suppliers are concluding agreements with Veikkaus in preparation for the new market. These early grants suggest that well-prepared applications are being processed, even as the permanent supervisory unit is still being staffed. Operators that have not yet applied should treat these examples as a signal that the queue is forming and that completeness of documentation will determine where they sit in it.

Mr Wallinheimo also raised a more fundamental question: whether the Finnish regulator will adopt a strict, Swedish-style supervisory culture or a more cooperative, Danish-style approach. The difference is significant. Spelinspektionen is known for formal enforcement, substantial sanctions and an expansive view of duty of care, while the Danish Gambling Authority has historically placed more emphasis on dialogue and guidance, although Denmark too is tightening its regime. A regulator that is under-resourced at launch may initially prioritise licensing over enforcement, but operators should not mistake early forbearance for the long-term posture.

The policy objectives explain why the Finnish authorities will be under pressure to show results. Channelisation is currently estimated at around 50 per cent, and the stated target is 90 per cent once private operators enter. Mr Wallinheimo cited between EUR 600 million and EUR 900 million in gambling revenue lost overseas. Achieving that channelisation shift requires both an attractive licensed offer and effective action against unlicensed operators, including payment blocking and marketing restrictions. A regulator that struggles to staff up may find it difficult to deliver the enforcement half of that equation, which in turn affects the commercial case for licensed entry.

Prospective licensees should plan on the assumption that the regulator will be stretched in its first year. That means filing complete, well-evidenced applications early; preparing detailed documentation on responsible gambling tools, identity verification, AML controls and Finnish-language customer communications; and ensuring that B2B suppliers in their supply chain are ready for the July 2027 supplier window. Operators should also build contingency into launch planning, including marketing commitments and sponsorship deals, in case licence decisions arrive later than hoped.

Finland's reform enjoys broad cross-party support, and there is no indication that the 1 July 2027 date is at risk politically. The risk is operational. Operators that engage early with the new unit, respond quickly to information requests and align their compliance frameworks with Nordic regulatory expectations will be best placed to launch on time. Nordic counsel experienced with the Swedish and Danish regimes can help applicants anticipate the supervisory culture that is likely to emerge.

A.title: Romania's ONJN Halts RON 25m Gambling Harm Programme
A.excerpt: Romania's ONJN has suspended its RON 25m Conscious and Free harm-prevention grants over budget and legal gaps. What it means for the sector.
body: Romania's National Gambling Office, the ONJN, has suspended its flagship harm-prevention funding programme, Conscious and Free, pending resolution of what it describes as legal and financial inconsistencies. The programme, worth RON 25 million, or roughly EUR 5.1 million, was to be financed from the regulator's own 2026 budget and was formally committed in a notice published in the Official Gazette in December 2025. The suspension was reported between 14 and 16 November 2026, months after preliminary results had been published on 28 July.

The scale of the programme explains why the decision has attracted attention. The ONJN received 199 project applications and evaluated 180. Applicants included organisations planning prevention, treatment and research work, many of which prepared staff, partners and service plans on the basis of the preliminary results. The regulator has stressed that this is a suspension rather than a cancellation and has said it intends to restructure the programme on a firmer legal and budgetary footing, but it has given no end date.

The reasons given are procedural. A newly formed working group reviewed the programme and concluded that the selected projects lacked a clear budgetary basis, that the rules did not make contracts conditional on first securing funds, leaving a gap between published results and available money, and that the implementation timeline was unworkable given how little of the budget year remained. None of these findings concerns the merit of individual projects, and the reports indicate no wrongdoing by applicants. They do, however, raise questions about how the programme was approved and published without those safeguards in place.

For applicants, the legal position will turn on the precise status of the preliminary results and the programme rules. If no funding contracts were concluded, applicants are unlikely to have enforceable rights to payment, and any claim would need to rest on public law principles such as legitimate expectation or administrative fairness. Where organisations incurred costs in reliance on published results, they should retain documentation and take advice on whether any remedy is available under Romanian administrative law. Whether any funds were paid out before the pause is one of several questions the ONJN has not yet answered.

Licensed operators are not directly affected. The reported suspension involves no change to licensing conditions or to operators' player protection obligations under Romanian law, which continue to apply in full. Operators should not interpret the pause as any relaxation of responsible gambling expectations; Romanian authorities have been tightening advertising and player protection rules, and harm prevention remains a political priority. Operators that participate in or fund harm-prevention initiatives voluntarily may wish to consider whether they can support affected organisations in the interim.

The episode carries a broader lesson for regulators across Europe that fund harm reduction from levies or their own budgets. In Great Britain, the statutory levy is being channelled through structured commissioning arrangements; in other markets, regulators and ministries are under pressure to show that money spent on research, prevention and treatment is properly governed and delivers measurable outcomes. Programmes that announce winners before funding and contracting mechanisms are secured create legal risk for the authority and reputational damage for the sector, and can undermine trust among the very organisations the money is meant to support.

For the Romanian market, the key next steps are publication of a restructured programme, a new budget line and timetable, and clarity on how the 180 evaluated projects will be treated, whether they are re-scored, invited to resubmit or carried over. Industry participants and harm-prevention organisations should monitor the ONJN's official notices for confirmation of the suspension's terms and any revised framework. Operators with a Romanian licence should continue to treat player protection compliance as a priority and keep their governance of any responsible gambling funding commitments under review.
